A refresh can break retrieval several ways: a re-index that failed partway leaving a mix of old and new content, an embedding regeneration that didn't complete so vectors no longer correspond to their text, a parser that mishandled a changed document format, or metadata that no longer matches. Inspecting the actual retrieved chunks for a failing query is the fastest way to confirm. B (silent weight update) isn't how versioned endpoints work and doesn't explain the timing. D (temperature) is stated unchanged and low temperature produces consistency, not fabrication. A (shrunken context window) would produce truncation/dropped content, and again nothing in the scenario changed there. Blueprint: diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch).

questions.text: A team is building the first evaluation set for a customer-email classification system before launch. Which composition is most appropriate?

options.text: 1,000 examples generated by a language model to cover the label space quickly.
The 50 emails the team found most interesting during development.
A random sample of production traffic with labels assigned by the system itself.

A set built primarily from real historical emails labelled by domain experts, deliberately including known edge cases, ambiguous items, and the rare-but-costly categories, with class balance recorded rather than artificially equalized.

questions.explanation: Correct: D. An evaluation set is only useful insofar as performance on it predicts performance in production, which requires real distributional characteristics and trustworthy labels. Expert-labelled historical emails give ground truth grounded in actual customer language. Deliberately including edge cases, ambiguous items, and rare-but-costly categories is what makes the set diagnostic — average accuracy on easy examples hides exactly the failures that matter. Recording rather than equalizing class balance keeps the metric interpretable (forcing a 2% category to 14% produces numbers that don't correspond to reality). A (synthetic as the primary basis) bakes the generating model's blind spots into the yardstick. B (50 dev-selected examples) is too small for confidence and biased toward cases the team already thought about. C (labelling production data with the system under test) is circular — it scores near-perfectly by construction; sampling production traffic is good, but the labels must come from an independent source. Blueprint: design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies.

questions.text: An architect is defining evaluation metrics for a production Claude system. Select TWO statements that reflect sound evaluation design.

options.text: Evaluation should be performed once before launch and repeated only if users complain.
Metrics should span quality, latency, cost, and safety, because optimizing any one alone can degrade the others.
Safety evaluation is only necessary for consumer-facing systems.
A single aggregate accuracy figure is sufficient if it is measured on a large enough sample.
Metrics should be segmented by meaningful slices — such as request type, customer tier, or language — because aggregate figures conceal localized failure.

questions.explanation: Correct: B and E. Sound evaluation is multi-dimensional and segmented. Multi-dimensional (B) because these systems have coupled properties: a change that raises accuracy may double latency or cost, and a change that reduces cost may weaken safety — measure only one and you optimize it into a regression elsewhere. Segmented (E) because aggregate metrics are averages, and averages hide concentrated harm — a system at 94% overall may be at 62% for one language or one high-value customer segment, invisible until that segment escalates. D (large sample) fixes statistical noise, not dimensional blindness. C (safety only for consumer-facing) is wrong — internal systems carry safety/security risk too (data leakage, prompt injection via ingested documents, harmful automation). A (once before launch, then on complaints) makes user complaints the detector — the slowest, most expensive, post-harm signal; behaviour, data, and usage all drift, so evaluation must be continuous. Blueprint: define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security).

questions.text: A team wants to compare two system prompts for a summarization feature. Summaries have no single correct answer, and the qualities that matter are faithfulness to the source and usefulness to the reader. Which evaluation methodology is most appropriate?

options.text: A mixed approach: programmatic checks for objective properties such as length limits and absence of fabricated entities, plus model-based grading against an explicit rubric, calibrated against a human-labelled subset.
Exact string matching against reference summaries written by the team.
Measure only average output length, since concise summaries are better.
Ask the model that produced each summary to rate its own quality.

questions.explanation: Correct: A. Open-ended generation requires layered evaluation because different qualities are best measured by different instruments. Deterministic code is perfect for objective, checkable properties — length limits, required sections, whether every named entity appears in the source — and it's fast and free. Faithfulness and usefulness are judgment calls, so a model-based grader against an explicit rubric scales the assessment. The calibration clause completes the answer: you validate the grader against a human-labelled subset, because an uncalibrated automated judge produces confident numbers of unknown correspondence to human opinion. B (exact string matching) assumes one correct output — a summary can be excellent and share almost no character sequences with the reference. D (self-rating by the generating model) is systematically biased toward its own output. C (length only) ignores content entirely — a short summary that omits the key finding is worse than a longer one that captures it. Blueprint: design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies.

questions.text: A team plans to A/B test a new prompt against the current one in production. Which experimental design flaw would most undermine the result?

options.text: Assigning users to variants at random rather than by geography.
Deploying the new prompt to variant B while simultaneously upgrading variant B's model and increasing its retrieval depth.
Running the test for two weeks rather than one.
Measuring both task success rate and cost per request.

questions.explanation: Correct: B. Changing three variables at once destroys attribution. If variant B performs better, you can't tell whether the prompt, the model upgrade, or the deeper retrieval is responsible — and if the changes interact, the individual effects may point in opposite directions, so you could ship a worse prompt because a model upgrade masked it. Controlled experiments isolate one variable; if multiple changes must be evaluated, they need separate arms or a factorial design. A (random assignment) is correct practice — assigning by geography would introduce confounds. C (two weeks vs one) generally improves statistical power and captures weekly seasonality — more defensible, not less. D (measuring both quality and cost) is sound multi-dimensional evaluation. Blueprint: conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements.

questions.text: A generation step costs more than budgeted. Profiling shows that 78% of input tokens come from a static instruction block and a fixed reference table sent identically on every request, and 22% from variable user content. Output tokens are modest. Which optimization has the greatest cost impact for the least quality risk?

options.text: Reduce the maximum output tokens.
Compress the variable user content before sending it.
Enable prompt caching on the static prefix so the repeated 78% is billed at the reduced cached rate rather than reprocessed on every call.
Remove the reference table and rely on the model's general knowledge.

questions.explanation: Correct: C. Optimization should target the largest cost component that can be reduced without losing information, and the profile hands you the answer: 78% of input tokens are byte-identical across requests. Caching that prefix means those tokens are written once and subsequently billed at a substantially reduced rate, with no content removed and therefore no quality risk — the model sees exactly the same input. It also reduces time-to-first-token as a bonus. The pairing of 'largest share' and 'identical every time' is the signal for caching. A (cap output) — output is modest, so the addressable saving is small, and capping risks truncation. D (delete the reference table) removes information the system was designed to use, trading correctness for cost — the opposite of least quality risk. B (compress the variable 22%) attacks the smaller share, and lossy compression of user content risks discarding the specifics the request depends on. Blueprint: optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs.

questions.text: A system that performed well at launch shows gradually declining user satisfaction over four months, while offline evaluation scores remain unchanged. What is the most probable explanation?

options.text: The evaluation set is too large to be sensitive to changes.
Users have become less tolerant of the same quality level.
The model has degraded over time through repeated use.
The production input distribution has drifted away from the fixed evaluation set, so the eval no longer represents real traffic.

questions.explanation: Correct: D. The contradiction between stable offline scores and falling real-world satisfaction is the defining symptom of distribution drift. A static evaluation set measures performance on the world as it was when the set was built; production traffic moves — new products, changed customer language, seasonal patterns, new use cases users discover on their own. The system may genuinely still be excellent at what the eval measures and poor at what users now send. The remedy is to refresh the evaluation set from recent production traffic on a schedule and to monitor input characteristics directly so drift is visible before satisfaction falls. C (model degrades through use) is false — a deployed model is a fixed artifact; usage doesn't wear it out. B (shifting expectations) is a weak, unfalsifiable explanation for a steady four-month decline and conveniently locates the problem outside the system. A (eval too large) is backwards — larger sets are generally more sensitive; size isn't the issue, representativeness is. Blueprint: monitor system performance using logging and observability tools; design evaluation datasets.

questions.text: An agent completes its task successfully in 91% of evaluation runs. In the 9% of failures, the team observes no common pattern in the final output. Which diagnostic approach is most likely to identify the root cause?

options.text: Examine the full execution traces of failing runs — tool calls, arguments, results, and intermediate reasoning — and compare them against traces of successful runs on similar inputs.
Replace the model with a larger one and re-measure.
Increase the evaluation set size until a pattern emerges in the outputs.
Re-run the failing cases with a higher temperature to see whether results improve.

questions.explanation: Correct: A. When failures share no visible pattern in the final output, the divergence happened earlier in the execution path. Traces expose where: a tool called with a malformed argument, a retrieval that returned nothing and was silently treated as empty rather than as an error, a loop that exhausted its budget, a reasoning step that made an unwarranted assumption. Comparing failing traces against successful traces on similar inputs is the key technique — it isolates the step at which the two diverge rather than leaving you to read traces in isolation. D (higher temperature) increases randomness; if some runs then succeed you've learned only that the failure is stochastic, not why, and you've made the system less predictable. C (more examples) produces more unexplained failures — volume doesn't substitute for visibility into intermediate state. B (swap the model) is a shot in the dark that may move the number without explaining it, and a larger model could intermittently mask a malformed tool argument, leaving a latent defect. Blueprint: diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch).

questions.text: A model-based grader (LLM-as-judge) is used to score answer quality at scale. Which practice most improves the trustworthiness of its scores?

options.text: Using the same model and prompt that generated the answers, for consistency.
Defining an explicit rubric with concrete criteria and score anchors, and periodically measuring the grader's agreement with human raters on a held-out subset.
Averaging scores across many runs at high temperature to reduce variance.
Asking the grader for a single overall score from 1 to 10 with no further guidance.

questions.explanation: Correct: B. A model-based grader is itself a measurement instrument, and instruments require specification and calibration. An explicit rubric with concrete criteria and score anchors — what distinguishes a 4 from a 5, with examples — converts a vague impression into a repeatable judgment and makes disagreements inspectable. Periodic agreement measurement against human raters is the calibration step: it tells you whether the grader's numbers actually track human judgment and catches drift when prompts or data change. Without it you have precise-looking scores of unknown validity. A (generating model/prompt as judge) introduces self-preference bias and shared blind spots — independence between generator and grader is desirable. D (unanchored 1-10) is the least reliable form of model grading — the scale means something different across runs and examples, with no way to audit a disagreement. C (average high-temperature runs) reduces variance around the grader's central tendency but does nothing about bias — a systematically wrong grader will be consistently, precisely wrong. Blueprint: design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies.

questions.text: A summarization system occasionally introduces facts that do not appear in the source document. Which combination of measures most directly reduces this failure?

options.text: Increase temperature to encourage more creative summaries.
Summarize the summary a second time to remove errors.

Instruct the model to base every statement on the source and to state when information is absent; add an automated faithfulness check that verifies claims and entities against the source; and route low-scoring outputs to review.
Increase the maximum output length so the model has room to be accurate.

questions.explanation: Correct: C. Fabrication is best attacked in layers. At the prompt level, explicitly grounding the task and — critically — giving the model a legitimate way to say information is absent removes the pressure to always produce a complete summary implicitly rewarding invention. At the verification level, an automated faithfulness check that traces claims and named entities back to the source detects what the prompt didn't prevent. At the operational level, routing low-scoring outputs to human review contains the residual. Prevention, detection, and containment together — the standard pattern for a probabilistic failure mode. A (higher temperature) increases sampling diversity, raising the likelihood of unsupported content — 'creative' is the opposite of faithful. D (fabrication isn't caused by insufficient output space) — more room to write is more room to invent. B (a second summarization pass) has no access to the source at that point, so it can't distinguish invented from real content and will happily preserve and even reinforce the fabrication. Blueprint: diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch); implement guardrails.

questions.text: A team must reduce the cost of a production Claude workload by 40% without a material quality regression. Select TWO approaches that are most consistent with disciplined optimization.

options.text: Profile where tokens are actually consumed, then cache stable prefixes and eliminate redundant context that adds no measured value.
Reduce the evaluation set size so that testing costs less.
Disable logging and tracing to reduce infrastructure spend.
Route simple requests to a smaller model and reserve the larger model for requests that evaluation shows genuinely require it.
Cap all responses at 100 tokens regardless of the request.

questions.explanation: Correct: A and D. Both are evidence-driven and preserve the ability to detect regression. Profiling first (A) separates optimization from guesswork — you find that a repeated prefix or an unused retrieved field dominates the bill, and you cache or remove it with no information loss. Tiered routing (D) exploits that request difficulty isn't uniform: most traffic is straightforward and doesn't need the largest model, and evaluation tells you where the boundary sits rather than intuition. Together they typically deliver large savings while leaving quality measurable. B (shrink the eval set) reduces your ability to detect the regression the requirement forbids, and saves trivial money since evaluation is a small fraction of production spend — cutting the instrument panel to save fuel. C (remove observability) destroys the diagnostic capability you most need while making cost/latency changes, and logging is a minor line item next to inference. E (blanket 100-token cap) is an indiscriminate quality cut that truncates any response legitimately requiring more, directly violating the no-material-regression constraint. Blueprint: optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs.

questions.text: A Claude-based assistant ingests customer-supplied documents and has tools that can send email and update CRM records. A security reviewer raises prompt injection as a concern. Which mitigation is most effective?

options.text: Use a larger model, which is more resistant to injection.
Instruct the model in its system prompt to ignore any instructions found inside customer documents.
Scan documents for the phrase "ignore previous instructions" and reject matches.

Treat all ingested content as untrusted data — clearly delimit it from instructions, constrain tool permissions to the minimum required, and require confirmation or policy checks before any outbound or state-changing action.

questions.explanation: Correct: D. Prompt injection is an architectural problem, not a prompting problem, because the model cannot reliably distinguish instructions from data when both arrive as text. The defensible answer assumes injection will sometimes succeed and limits what a successful injection can accomplish: delimiting untrusted content reduces the probability; constraining tool permissions bounds the blast radius; and gating outbound email and CRM writes behind confirmation or policy checks means the dangerous step — the one that causes harm outside the system — requires an authorization the injected instruction cannot supply. The combination of tool access and untrusted input is what makes this high risk. B (a system-prompt instruction) is a probabilistic defence against an adversary actively crafting text to defeat it — worth including as one layer, but relying on it alone makes your security boundary a suggestion. C (signature matching on a known phrase) is trivially evaded by rewording, encoding, translating, or splitting the payload. A (larger model) does not confer immunity — a more capable model may follow a sophisticated injected instruction more competently; capability is not a security control. Blueprint: identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems; implement guardrails and safety controls.

questions.text: A healthcare provider wants a Claude application that summarizes patient records for clinicians. Which consideration must be resolved before the architecture is finalized?

options.text: The regulatory basis for processing protected health information — deployment location and data residency, the business associate relationship, retention and logging of PHI, access controls, and the audit trail — established with legal and compliance before build.
Whether the interface will be web-based or embedded in the EHR.
How many clinicians will use the system in the first quarter.
Which Claude model produces the most fluent summaries.

questions.explanation: Correct: A. In regulated domains, compliance constraints are architectural inputs, not features added later. Where the data may be processed and stored determines the deployment platform; the business associate relationship determines whether the processing is permissible at all; PHI retention and logging rules determine what your observability stack may capture (a design decision that is painful to retrofit); and access controls and audit trails shape the identity propagation model. Discovering any of these after the build means rework at best and an unlaunchable system at worst. D (fluency) is a quality attribute selected by evaluation once the compliant design space is known — it can't drive a decision that may be foreclosed by data-residency requirements. B (interface placement) is a legitimate design question but downstream of whether and where PHI may be processed. C (user volume) informs capacity and cost, not legal permissibility — a system that can't lawfully process PHI doesn't become acceptable at low volume. Blueprint: ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP).

questions.text: A hiring-support tool uses Claude to summarize candidate applications and highlight relevant experience. Which governance measure most directly addresses fairness risk?

options.text: Adding a disclaimer to each summary stating that it was generated by AI.

Evaluating outputs for systematic differences across demographic groups on matched candidate profiles, restricting the model's access to protected attributes and their close proxies, and documenting the assessment as part of a periodic review.
Using the largest available model, which is more capable and therefore fairer.
Requiring recruiters to read every summary before making a decision.

questions.explanation: Correct: B. Fairness must be measured to be managed, and the measurement technique matters: comparing outputs across matched profiles that differ only in group membership isolates disparate treatment from legitimate differences in qualification. Restricting access to protected attributes and their proxies — names, addresses, graduation years, affiliations that correlate with protected characteristics — reduces the pathway by which bias enters. Documenting the assessment on a recurring schedule turns a one-time check into governance, which is what regulators and internal risk functions will ask to see (employment decisions are high-scrutiny in most jurisdictions). D (human review) is a valuable control but doesn't address bias in the summary itself — a recruiter reading a systematically skewed summary inherits the skew, and people under-correct for biased inputs presented as neutral analysis. C (capability and fairness are independent) — a more capable model can reproduce societal bias more articulately. A (disclosure) is a transparency measure that informs the reader without changing the content. Blueprint: address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency).

questions.text: An architect is documenting the failure modes of a proposed Claude system for a risk review. Select TWO failure modes that are inherent characteristics of LLM-based systems and must be designed for rather than eliminated.

options.text: The system will exceed its monthly budget if usage grows.
The system will fail if the network connection to the API is unavailable.
The system may produce fluent, confident output that is factually incorrect.
The system requires a valid API key to operate.
The system may return different outputs for semantically identical inputs across runs.

questions.explanation: Correct: C and E. Both are intrinsic to how language models work rather than defects to be patched. Fluent-but-wrong output (C) follows from a system that generates plausible continuations rather than retrieving verified facts; you manage it with grounding, citation, verification, and human review at the points where being wrong is costly. Non-determinism (E) follows from probabilistic sampling; you manage it by designing for tolerance — validating output against schemas, making downstream steps idempotent, and setting expectations that identical inputs need not produce identical text. Naming these honestly in a risk review distinguishes a credible architect from an optimistic one. B (network dependency) is an ordinary distributed-systems concern addressed with retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, and fallbacks — not specific to LLMs. A (budget overrun) is a cost-management issue handled with quotas, alerting, and rate limits — a consequence of usage, not a model behaviour. D (credential requirement) is a normal access-control property, not a failure mode. Blueprint: identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems.

questions.text: A European retailer plans a Claude-based service that processes customer contact history to generate personalized recommendations. Which GDPR-related design decision is most material to the architecture?

options.text: Ensuring the model was trained only on European data.
Translating the user interface into all supported European languages.

Establishing the lawful basis and purpose limitation for the processing, and designing for data subject rights — access, rectification, erasure — including what personal data enters prompts, what is retained in logs, and for how long.
Hosting the application behind a European domain name.

questions.explanation: Correct: C. GDPR obligations translate into concrete architectural constraints. Lawful basis and purpose limitation determine whether contact history may be used for recommendations at all and bound what else it may be used for. Data subject rights are the part teams most often overlook in LLM systems: if a customer requests erasure, you must be able to find and remove their personal data wherever it landed — which includes prompt logs, trace data, evaluation datasets built from production traffic, and any caches. Designing logging and retention with that requirement in mind from the start is far cheaper than retrofitting deletion into an observability stack built to keep everything. B (localization) is a product/accessibility concern — GDPR governs personal data processing, not interface language. D (a domain name) has no legal significance for data protection; what matters is where processing occurs, under what basis, with what safeguards. A confuses a real concern (where this system's data is processed and stored) with an unrelated one (the geographic provenance of a foundation model's training corpus). Blueprint: ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP).

questions.text: An agentic system can execute actions with real-world consequences: sending customer communications, issuing refunds, and modifying inventory. Which control design best balances autonomy with risk containment?

options.text: Allow full autonomy during business hours only.
Allow full autonomy, with a daily report of all actions taken.
Require human approval for every action the agent proposes.

Tier actions by reversibility and blast radius — allow low-impact reversible actions autonomously, require approval for high-impact or irreversible ones, and enforce rate limits and value ceilings on the autonomous tier.

questions.explanation: Correct: D. Autonomy should be granted in proportion to the cost of being wrong, and the two dimensions that determine that cost are reversibility and blast radius. An action that affects one record and can be undone in seconds doesn't warrant the same gate as an irreversible action affecting thousands. Tiering preserves the efficiency case for automation on the common low-impact path while placing a human at the points where errors are expensive or permanent. The rate limits and value ceilings are the essential backstop: they bound the damage from a systematic failure that produces many individually-approved-looking actions — the failure mode behind the most severe agentic incidents. C (approve everything) eliminates the automation benefit and, at volume, degrades into rubber-stamping. B (a daily report) is purely detective and arrives up to 24 hours late — refunds and communications can't be recalled once issued. A (business hours only) — time of day is unrelated to risk; a destructive action at 2 p.m. is exactly as destructive as at 2 a.m. Blueprint: implement guardrails and safety controls; apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies.

questions.text: A financial services client asks how the organization will demonstrate to regulators that its Claude-based advisory tool behaved appropriately on a specific past transaction. Which architectural capability is required?

options.text: Durable, tamper-evident audit records linking each interaction to the inputs, retrieved context, prompt and model versions, tool calls, output, and any human review — retained for the regulatory period.
A copy of the model's training data.
A statement from the model provider that the model is accurate.
High availability across multiple regions.

questions.explanation: Correct: A. Regulatory defensibility requires reconstructing what the system did and why, for a specific interaction, potentially years later. That means capturing the full decision context — not just the output but the inputs, the retrieved passages that grounded it, the exact prompt and model versions in force at that moment, the tools invoked, and any human review or override. Version capture is the detail candidates most often miss: without it you cannot reproduce the behaviour, because the prompt has since changed. Tamper-evidence and retention aligned to the regulatory period complete the requirement. B (training data) is neither available nor relevant to what happened in one interaction — regulators ask what the system did with this customer's information on this date. C (a vendor assurance) is not evidence about a specific transaction; no provider statement substitutes for your own records of your own system's behaviour. D (multi-region availability) is a resilience property with no bearing on demonstrating past behaviour. Blueprint: ensure compliance with regulations; analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale.

questions.text: A team proposes storing all production prompts and completions indefinitely in a general-purpose logging platform accessible to the whole engineering organization, to help with debugging. The system handles customer financial data. What is the most significant governance objection?

options.text: Storing completions will make the evaluation set easier to build.

Prompts and completions will contain customer financial data, so the logging platform inherits the data's sensitivity and requires equivalent access control, retention limits, and deletion capability — broad access and indefinite retention are a data protection failure.
Log storage costs will grow over time.
Logs in a general-purpose platform may be harder to query than in a purpose-built tool.

questions.explanation: Correct: B. The critical insight is that observability data for an LLM system is not metadata — the prompts and completions are the customer data, reproduced in full. That makes the logging platform a system of record for regulated financial information, so it must inherit every control that applies to the source: restricted access on a need-to-know basis rather than organization-wide, defined retention rather than indefinite, and the ability to locate and delete a specific customer's data on request. Broad engineering access to production financial data is also an access-control violation independent of retention, and the two together would likely fail an audit. C (storage cost) is real but minor and economic, not governance — it wouldn't block the design. D (queryability) is an ergonomics issue about how pleasant debugging is, not whether the arrangement is permissible. A names a genuine benefit — building evaluation sets from production traffic is good practice — but it must happen within the same access and retention controls; it isn't an objection. Blueprint: ensure compliance with regulations; analyze observability challenges.

questions.text: During design review of a medical triage support tool, a stakeholder asks how the system will handle questions outside its validated scope, such as a user describing symptoms of a possible emergency. What is the appropriate design response?

options.text: Return a generic error message for any input the system does not recognize.
Log the request for later review and provide a best-effort answer in the meantime.

Define explicit out-of-scope behaviour: recognize the condition, decline to advise, and route to the defined escalation path with clear urgent-care guidance — enforced with both prompt-level instruction and programmatic detection, and validated by evaluation.
Allow the model to answer using its general medical knowledge, since it is broadly capable.

questions.explanation: Correct: C. Scope boundaries in safety-critical domains must be designed, enforced, and tested rather than assumed. The design has three necessary parts: the system must recognize the out-of-scope condition, decline to give advice it isn't validated to give, and — crucially — take a positive action by routing to the escalation path with urgent-care guidance, because a bare refusal to someone describing emergency symptoms is itself a harm. Enforcing at both the prompt level and programmatically reflects that this is too important to rest on a probabilistic control, and validating with evaluation confirms the behaviour actually fires on realistic inputs. D (general capability is not clinical validation) — answering outside the validated scope in a medical context creates patient-safety risk and regulatory exposure regardless of how plausible the answer sounds. A (a generic error) abandons a user who may be in an emergency and fails to distinguish an unrecognized input from a recognized-but-urgent one. B ('best-effort answer' is precisely what must not happen here, and deferred logging means review arrives long after any harm) — this inverts the correct ordering: act safely now, review later. Blueprint: implement guardrails and safety controls; apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies.

questions.text: An organization is establishing governance for Claude systems across many teams. Which approach best balances consistency with delivery speed?

options.text: Require a central architecture board to review and approve every prompt change before deployment.
Standardize on a single system prompt used by every team's application.
Allow each team full autonomy and address problems as they arise.

Publish shared standards — approved patterns, reusable guardrail components, evaluation requirements, and a risk-tiering rubric — and reserve central review for systems that the rubric classifies as high risk.

questions.explanation: Correct: D. Effective governance scales by making the safe path the easy path. Publishing approved patterns, reusable guardrail components, and clear evaluation requirements lets most teams comply by default without waiting for anyone. A risk-tiering rubric then concentrates scarce central review where consequences justify it — systems touching regulated data, taking irreversible actions, or facing customers — so oversight is proportionate rather than uniform. This is risk-tiered human review applied at the organizational level. A (review every prompt change) creates a bottleneck that scales linearly with adoption and will be routed around as soon as it becomes painful — governance teams evade provides less real assurance. C (full autonomy with reactive correction) guarantees inconsistent controls and makes the first serious incident the discovery mechanism. B (a single shared system prompt across different applications) is not achievable — a fraud triage tool and an internal HR assistant have genuinely different tasks; sharing a module of common policy language is the workable version, which is a different thing. Blueprint: implement guardrails and safety controls; support lifecycle phases.

questions.text: A client opens a discovery session by saying, "We want to use AI to improve customer service." What is the most effective next step for the architect?

options.text: Run structured discovery to establish the current process, its measurable pain points, what success would look like numerically, what constraints exist, and who owns the outcome.
Propose a reference architecture for a customer service assistant based on similar past engagements.
Request access to the client's ticketing system so the data can be analyzed immediately.
Ask which Claude model the client would prefer to use.

questions.explanation: Correct: A. 'Improve customer service' is an aspiration, not a requirement. Structured discovery converts it into something buildable by establishing the current process and its actual failure points, a quantified definition of success (deflection rate, first-response time, CSAT — with a target), the constraints that bound the solution space (regulatory, data residency, systems that cannot be changed, budget), and crucially who owns the outcome and will make decisions. Skipping this is the most common cause of projects that deliver working software nobody adopts, because the team solved the problem they assumed rather than the one that exists. B (proposing an architecture first) imports assumptions from a different client's context and anchors the conversation on a solution, making it socially awkward for the client to reveal facts that would invalidate it. D (model selection) is a late, evaluation-driven decision that depends on requirements not yet known. C (data analysis) is valuable but premature, and requesting production data access before any purpose is established raises governance questions. Blueprint: conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering.

questions.text: An executive sponsor asks why the proposed system uses retrieval rather than "just having the AI learn our documents." Which explanation is most effective for this audience?

options.text: Explain the mathematics of embedding spaces and vector similarity search.

Explain that retrieval lets the assistant look up the current document at the moment of the question — so updates take effect immediately, answers can cite their source, and there is no retraining cost or delay when policies change.
State that retrieval is the industry-standard approach for enterprise deployments.
Explain that training a model on the documents is technically impossible.

questions.explanation: Correct: B. Effective communication with a non-technical sponsor translates architecture into consequences the sponsor cares about, using an accurate mental model rather than a simplified-to-the-point-of-wrong one. 'Looks it up when asked' is both true and immediately intuitive, and it yields three business-relevant implications: changes take effect at once, answers are attributable to a source the business can verify, and there is no retraining cycle or cost each time policy changes. The sponsor can now evaluate the decision rather than merely defer to it. A (embedding mathematics) answers a question the sponsor didn't ask — correct but unusable information erodes confidence, since the sponsor concludes the architect can't explain the decision. C (an appeal to industry standard) is an argument from authority that gives the sponsor no basis for judgment and collapses the moment someone asks why it's standard. D is false — models can be trained on documents; winning an objection with an inaccurate claim is a credibility risk that one informed person in the room can unravel. Blueprint: communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs.

questions.text: Evaluation shows a proposed document classification system will be correct about 93% of the time. The business sponsor expects "AI accuracy," which they describe as near-perfect. What is the most appropriate way to handle this expectation gap?

options.text: Delay the conversation until the system is in production and the sponsor observes the error rate directly.
Report the system's accuracy on its best-performing category to build confidence.

Present the 93% figure early alongside the current human baseline, the cost profile of each error type, and the design's containment measures — then agree an accuracy target and a review path as part of the SLA.
Commit to 99% accuracy and treat closing the gap as an engineering problem to be solved later.

questions.explanation: Correct: C. The gap is between an expectation and a measured reality, best closed with context rather than concealment or capitulation. The human baseline is the essential comparison — if the existing manual process is 89% accurate, 93% is an improvement rather than a shortfall, and sponsors routinely hold automated systems to a standard they never applied to people. Error-cost profiling reframes the discussion productively, since a 7% error rate concentrated in cheap, easily corrected cases is very different from 7% concentrated in expensive ones. Ending with an agreed target and review path in the SLA converts a vague expectation into a shared, measurable commitment. A (defer a known gap) guarantees the conversation happens at the worst moment — after launch, in front of an unhappy sponsor, with trust already damaged. B (presenting the best-performing slice as though it were overall performance) is misleading by selection; when the real number surfaces, credibility on every other claim goes with it. D (committing to a number you have no evidence you can reach) creates a contractual obligation on a hope. Blueprint: manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs).

questions.text: An architect is preparing handoff documentation for the client's internal team, who will own the system after go-live. Select TWO items that are most essential to include.

options.text: The personal contact details of each consultant who worked on the project.
The evaluation suite and its baseline results, with instructions for running it and interpreting a regression.
The rationale behind key architectural decisions, including options considered and why they were rejected.
A transcript of every design meeting held during the engagement.
A list of every Claude model available at the time of writing.

questions.explanation: Correct: B and C. These are the two artifacts that determine whether the receiving team can safely change the system. The evaluation suite with baselines (B) is the safety net: without a way to run tests and recognize a regression, the new owners must either freeze the system or change it blind — both failure modes. Decision rationale including rejected options (C) prevents the most predictable post-handoff mistake — a new owner 'fixing' something that was a deliberate trade-off, then rediscovering the original problem the hard way. Recording why an option was rejected is what makes the document durable, because it answers the question the next engineer will actually have. D (raw meeting transcripts) is unfiltered volume — the signal it contains is exactly what C captures in usable form; the rest is noise that makes the documentation less likely to be read. E (a model catalogue) is public, freely available, and stale within months — documentation should record what your system does and why, not restate the vendor's product list. A (individual contact details) is not a support model — handoff should define a supported escalation path and ownership, which survives people changing jobs. Blueprint: document architectures and provide implementation guidance; support lifecycle phases.

questions.text: Three weeks into a build, the client's operations lead reveals a regulatory constraint requiring all customer data to remain within a specific jurisdiction — a constraint that invalidates the chosen deployment platform. What does this most clearly indicate about the engagement?

options.text: The team should proceed and seek a compliance exception.
The client's regulatory environment is unusually complex.
The operations lead should have volunteered the information earlier.
Discovery did not systematically surface regulatory and data residency constraints, and did not include all stakeholders who hold binding requirements.

questions.explanation: Correct: D. Data residency is a standard discovery question, not an exotic one, and its absence points to a process failure the architect owns. Two things went wrong: the discovery checklist didn't systematically probe regulatory and data-location constraints, and the stakeholder map omitted someone who holds binding requirements. Constraints that can invalidate a platform choice must be gathered before that choice is made, which means identifying everyone with veto power — legal, compliance, security, operations — during discovery rather than encountering them mid-build. Treating this as a process defect is what prevents recurrence. C (blaming the stakeholder) is unproductive and misplaced — domain experts don't know which of the hundreds of facts they hold are architecturally significant; eliciting them is the architect's job, and a good process assumes stakeholders won't self-identify their constraints. B (framing an ordinary constraint as unusual complexity) avoids the lesson — jurisdictional data residency is common across financial services, healthcare, and the public sector. A (proceeding against a known constraint while hoping for an exception) is a serious governance failure — exceptions are granted before the fact by those authorized to grant them. Blueprint: conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering; support lifecycle phases.

questions.text: A client insists on an agentic architecture because a competitor announced one, although discovery shows their process is a fixed, well-understood five-step sequence. How should the architect respond?

options.text: Present the comparison on the client's own terms — what each option costs, how each performs, how each is tested and debugged — and recommend the workflow, while designing clear extension points should genuinely variable cases emerge.
Build the agentic system as requested, since the client is paying and has stated a preference.
Build the workflow but describe it as agentic in project documentation.
Refuse the engagement on the grounds that the requested architecture is inappropriate.

questions.explanation: Correct: A. The architect's obligation is to inform the decision, not to win the argument or defer to it. Presenting cost, performance, testability, and debuggability in the client's own terms gives them a basis to choose, and clients who arrived at a preference through market signals usually update readily once the trade-offs are concrete. The extension-points clause is what makes this collaborative rather than dismissive: it acknowledges the client's underlying concern — that the process may not stay fixed — and designs for it, so the recommendation is not simply 'you are wrong.' B (build a known-inappropriate architecture without objection) abdicates the advisory role the client is paying for; when it costs more and proves harder to debug, the client will reasonably ask why nobody said so. D (refusal) is a disproportionate response to a disagreement that hasn't yet been discussed, and a failure of the influencing skill the role requires — architects routinely change minds by presenting evidence. C (misrepresenting what was built) is an integrity failure that also creates a concrete future problem: the documentation misleads whoever maintains the system, and the deception surfaces the moment anyone technical reads the code. Blueprint: communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs; manage stakeholder expectation alignment.

questions.text: A Claude system has been live for six months. Which practice best reflects sound lifecycle management in the operate-and-iterate phase?

options.text: Rebuilding on the newest available model each time one is released.
Reviewing production monitoring and feedback on a defined cadence, refreshing the evaluation set from recent traffic, and running proposed changes through evaluation before deployment.
Rewriting the system prompt monthly to keep it current.
Leaving the system unchanged unless users report a defect, to avoid destabilizing a working deployment.

questions.explanation: Correct: B. Operate-and-iterate is a disciplined cycle, not a state of rest or of constant churn. Reviewing monitoring and feedback on a cadence means quality problems are found by the team rather than reported by users. Refreshing the evaluation set from recent production traffic keeps the yardstick aligned with reality as usage drifts — a static eval slowly stops measuring anything relevant. Gating every proposed change through evaluation before deployment is what allows the system to improve without regressing, which is the balance the phase requires. D (wait for defect reports) makes users the monitoring system and ignores drift entirely — the world changes even when the code doesn't, so an untouched system degrades in effectiveness over time. A (reflexive adoption of every new model) is change without evidence — a model upgrade is a significant variable that should be evaluated against your own task before adoption, since newer doesn't automatically mean better for your workload, cost profile, or latency budget. C (a calendar-driven prompt rewrite) is change for its own sake — prompts should change in response to evaluation findings, not the month. Blueprint: support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration).

questions.text: An architect must define an SLA for a Claude-based system with an external client. Which set of commitments is most defensible?

options.text: A guarantee that the system will produce correct answers 100% of the time.
A commitment to always use the most advanced model available.
Availability, latency percentiles, and a defined support and escalation process, with quality expressed as a measured accuracy target on an agreed evaluation set, reviewed on a stated cadence.
A commitment that the system will never require human review.

questions.explanation: Correct: C. A defensible SLA commits only to things that are measurable, controllable, and objectively verifiable by both parties. Availability and latency percentiles are standard and monitorable. The important nuance is how quality is expressed: not as a promise of correctness but as a target measured on an agreed evaluation set, which makes the commitment testable and gives both sides a shared definition of 'good.' The stated review cadence acknowledges that inputs and expectations evolve, providing a structured path to revisit the target rather than an argument later. A (guarantee 100% correctness) — no probabilistic system can guarantee it, and committing creates a term breached on day one, signalling to a sophisticated client that the architect misunderstands the technology. D (promising to eliminate human review) forecloses a control the design may require for high-risk actions, forcing the team to remove a safety mechanism to satisfy a contract. B ('most advanced available') commits to a moving target set by a third party, may conflict with cost/latency obligations in the same agreement, and confuses an input with an outcome. Blueprint: manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs).

questions.text: A pilot deployment succeeded, but adoption stalls after the general rollout: usage falls to 15% of eligible staff within a month. Investigation shows the system works as designed. What is the most likely gap?

options.text: The model is not capable enough for real work.
The system needs a more visually appealing interface.
Staff need to be instructed by management to use the system.
Change management and workflow integration — users were not brought into the design, the tool sits outside their existing workflow, and no one has addressed what the change means for how they work.

questions.explanation: Correct: D. When a system works as designed but nobody uses it, the failure is in adoption rather than engineering. Two causes dominate. First, workflow fit: a tool that requires leaving the application where the work actually happens imposes a switching cost that outweighs its benefit for most tasks, regardless of quality. Second, change management: users who weren't consulted during design have no ownership of the outcome, may not understand what the tool is for, and often carry unaddressed concerns about what it means for their role. Both are the architect's concern, because lifecycle management extends past deployment into realized value. A (capability) — the scenario states the system works and the pilot succeeded, so capability is the one thing demonstrated. B (visual polish) rarely drives adoption on its own and is a shallow diagnosis when workflow placement and change management are unexamined. C (mandated usage) produces compliance behaviour rather than value — people open the tool, do the minimum, and continue as before, and it suppresses the feedback signal since the usage metric no longer reflects genuine utility. Blueprint: support lifecycle phases; manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment.

questions.text: A client asks the architect to quantify the cost of a proposed Claude system before the design is finalized. Which response is most professional and useful?

options.text: Provide a modelled range based on expected request volume, estimated tokens per request, and candidate model pricing — stating the assumptions explicitly, identifying which are most uncertain, and committing to refine the estimate after prototype measurement.
Provide the lowest plausible figure to keep the project viable.
Provide the highest plausible figure so that actual costs compare favourably.
Decline to estimate until the design is complete and measured.

questions.explanation: Correct: A. Clients need a number to plan against, and architects can supply one honestly by modelling from the drivers — volume, tokens per request, model pricing — and being explicit about the assumptions underneath. Stating a range rather than a point communicates real uncertainty, flagging which assumptions are most uncertain tells the client where the risk sits and what would narrow it, and committing to refine after prototype measurement gives a defined path to a firmer figure. This is how a professional handles a question they can't yet answer precisely. D (refusing to estimate) is unhelpful and leaves the client unable to plan or secure budget — uncertainty is a reason to qualify an estimate, not to withhold one. B (deliberate underestimation to secure approval) is a form of misrepresentation and reliably produces the worst downstream conversation when actual costs arrive. C (padding to guarantee a favourable comparison) is equally dishonest and may kill a viable project outright, or damage credibility when the client benchmarks the figure elsewhere. Blueprint: communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs; manage stakeholder expectation alignment.

questions.text: An engineering organization is rolling out Claude Code across twelve teams working in a shared monorepo. Each team has different testing commands, code standards, and review conventions. What configuration approach best supports consistent, effective use?

options.text: Require every engineer to paste their team's conventions into each session manually.

Commit project-level configuration to the repository — repository-wide context at the root and team- or directory-scoped configuration in the relevant subdirectories — so conventions load automatically based on where work happens.
Maintain a shared wiki page documenting conventions and ask engineers to consult it.
Standardize all twelve teams on identical testing commands and conventions.

questions.explanation: Correct: B. Configuration that lives in the repository is version-controlled, reviewed like code, and — most importantly — applied automatically rather than depending on each engineer remembering. The hierarchical arrangement matches the actual structure of the problem: organization-wide standards at the root and team-specific conventions scoped to the directories that team owns, so an engineer working in any part of the monorepo gets the right context without configuring anything. Conventions also stay correct over time, because they're updated in the same pull request as the change that alters them. A (manual pasting) is unreliable at any scale, wastes context every session, and drifts immediately — engineers paste whatever version they last copied. C (a wiki) documents conventions for humans but doesn't supply them to the tool, and decays since nothing forces an update when the build commands change. D (forcing twelve teams onto identical conventions) is an organizational upheaval to solve a configuration problem, and the differences may be legitimate — a data pipeline team and a frontend team have genuinely different testing needs. Blueprint: configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code).

questions.text: A team wants an AI-assisted workflow that automatically runs the linter and type checker after each code edit, blocking the change if either fails. Which mechanism is designed for this?

options.text: A scheduled nightly job that lints the whole repository.
Manually running the linter after each session.
A deterministic hook that executes on the edit event and enforces the checks programmatically, independent of the model's judgment.
Adding a note to the system prompt asking the assistant to remember to lint.

questions.explanation: Correct: C. The requirement contains the words 'automatically' and 'blocking,' which together demand a deterministic enforcement point rather than a probabilistic one. A hook fires on a defined edit event and either passes or fails, so the guarantee holds on every edit regardless of what the model decides to do. This is a general principle worth internalizing: when a rule must always hold, implement it in code and place it in the execution path; reserve prompt instructions for guidance where occasional deviation is tolerable. D (a prompt-level reminder) is a request, not an enforcement, and will fail exactly when the session is long or complex — which is when it matters most. B (manual execution) is neither automatic nor blocking, and relies on the engineer remembering after the work feels finished. A (a nightly job) detects problems up to a day after they're introduced, by which time the change may be merged and built upon, and it cannot block — so it fails the stated requirement outright. Blueprint: improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling.

questions.text: An on-call engineer is debugging an intermittent production failure in a Claude-powered service. Which practice most improves the effectiveness of AI-assisted debugging?

options.text: Describing the symptom in general terms and asking for likely causes.
Asking the assistant to rewrite the affected module from scratch.
Increasing the assistant's context window setting to the maximum available.

Providing the concrete evidence — the failing session trace, the exact error output, the relevant configuration, and what distinguishes failing runs from passing ones — and asking for hypotheses ranked by how they can be tested.

questions.explanation: Correct: D. AI-assisted debugging is bounded by the evidence supplied. Concrete artifacts — the actual trace, the verbatim error, the configuration in force, and the contrast between failing and passing runs — let the assistant reason about the specific system rather than about systems in general. Asking for hypotheses ranked by testability is the second half of the technique: it produces a diagnostic plan you can execute in order, which matters under on-call pressure where an intermittent failure gives limited reproduction opportunities. A (a general symptom description) yields a general list of common causes, most of which don't apply — it reads as productive while advancing the investigation very little. B (rewriting the module) without understanding the failure may coincidentally remove the bug or preserve it in new code, and either way takes a large, unreviewed change into production during an incident — and you learn nothing, so recurrence is likely. C (context capacity) is not the constraint; the absence of relevant information is — a larger window with no evidence in it is still empty. Blueprint: support debugging and operational issue resolution.

questions.text: A platform team wants to make an internal deployment runbook — its steps, safety checks, environment-specific parameters, and helper scripts — available to engineers through their AI tooling, without every engineer configuring it individually. Which packaging approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Package it as a shared Skill committed to the repository, so it is version-controlled, discovered automatically, and loaded only when a deployment task is underway.
Add the full runbook to the system prompt of every internal tool.
Email the runbook to all engineers and ask them to paste relevant sections when needed.
Have each engineer maintain a personal copy adapted to their own preferences.

questions.explanation: Correct: A. The scenario describes exactly what Skills package: procedural instructions plus reference parameters plus executable helper scripts, bundled as one unit. Committing it to the repository makes it shared by default and version-controlled, so a change to the deployment process is reviewed and propagates to everyone at once. Automatic discovery removes per-engineer configuration, and on-demand loading means the runbook consumes no context for the overwhelming majority of sessions that have nothing to do with deployment. C (email distribution) guarantees version drift the moment the runbook changes, and manual pasting is exactly the per-engineer effort the requirement excludes. B (embedding the full runbook in every internal tool's system prompt) imposes its context cost on all work universally, and collapses entirely once the team has a dozen such runbooks. D (personal adapted copies) produces as many versions of the deployment process as there are engineers — the worst possible outcome for a procedure whose safety checks exist to prevent production incidents. Blueprint: configure Claude tools and environments for teams; implement prompt reuse strategies (Skills).

questions.text: An organization is measuring whether AI-assisted development tooling is delivering value. Select TWO measurement approaches that provide meaningful signal.

options.text: Measuring the number of prompts submitted per engineer per day.
Counting the number of lines of code generated by the assistant.
Requiring each engineer to report the hours they believe the assistant saved them.
Tracking delivery outcomes such as cycle time, change failure rate, and time to restore, compared against a pre-adoption baseline.
Combining outcome metrics with structured developer feedback on where the tooling helps and where it creates rework.

questions.explanation: Correct: D and E. Value should be measured at the level of outcomes the business cares about, and delivery metrics benchmarked against a pre-adoption baseline (D) do that — cycle time, change failure rate, and time to restore capture whether work is actually shipping faster and more safely, and the baseline is what makes the comparison meaningful. Pairing those with structured developer feedback (E) supplies the causal story the numbers lack: where the tooling genuinely helps, and where it produces code that looks fine but generates rework downstream. Quantitative and qualitative together prevent both blind spots. B (lines of code) is a discredited productivity proxy and actively perverse for AI tooling — generating more code is often the failure mode, since verbose or duplicated code raises maintenance cost. A (prompt volume) measures activity, not value — high prompt counts may equally indicate the tooling is working well or that engineers are struggling to get a usable result. C (self-reported time savings) is subject to well-documented estimation bias in both directions, can't be validated, and creates an incentive to justify the tool's cost, contaminating the data. Blueprint: improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling.
